questions.prompt: You short $42,740 of stock A for 6 days at a borrow fee of 30% a year, charged at 1/360 of the yearly rate per day. What does the fee cost?
questions.explanation: The fee is a yearly rate charged per day: 42,740 × 0.30 × 6 / 360 = $213.70. On a $930 gain, that takes about 23%.

questions.prompt: Halfway through a pairs trade, the lender recalls the shares of your short leg and your broker cannot borrow them elsewhere. What happens?
options: The lender pays you the remaining expected profit
You must buy the shares back and close the short leg, even if the spread is still far from its mean
Nothing changes until the z-score returns near 0
The borrow fee drops to zero for the rest of the trade
questions.explanation: A recall means returning the shares now. Buying them back closes the short leg early, which can lock in a loss while the gap is still open.

questions.prompt: Two pairs have the same expected gain per trade. Pair X has a half-life of 5 days and pair Y a half-life of 40 days. Both short legs cost 20% a year to borrow. Which statement is right?
options: Y pays more in borrow fees, because its trades hold the short leg for more days
Both pay the same fee, because the rate is the same
X pays more, because it trades faster
Neither pays a fee, because a pairs trade is hedged
questions.explanation: The fee is charged for each day the short leg is open. A slower spread keeps trades open longer, so more days pay the same daily fee.
